name: Severity calibration and needs-validation discipline in a plugin audit
query: Our automated scanner flagged two 'High' issues in our custom page-builder plugin and the client wants a findings report with severities. Issue 1: the 'Custom HTML' block saves raw HTML to post meta without kses; the save handler checks check_admin_referer( 'pb_save' ) and current_user_can( 'unfiltered_html' ) first. Issue 2: the image importer copies a remote file into wp-content/uploads/pb/ keeping the original extension after checking only that the MIME header says image/*; the importer is reachable by users with upload_files. We host on managed hosting but I don't know their server config. Please rate both.
expected_behavior: Treat the request as a full review with a findings report: record review context (target, immutable revision, scope, testing authorization, limitations) with unavailable values explicitly Unknown.

For issue 1, trace the save handler and recognize that only principals with unfiltered_html reach the raw-HTML write, so storing script is authority WordPress already grants them; check whether any lower-trust principal (contributor, multisite site admin without unfiltered_html) or another write path reaches the same meta before deciding.

If no lower-trust path exists, do not report issue 1 as a vulnerability: record it as rejected with the governing current_user_can( 'unfiltered_html' ) control, or as hardening at most, and give it no severity.

For issue 2, trace the importer: an author-level principal (upload_files) controls the remote file and the saved extension, and the MIME header check does not validate the extension or content, so a .php or .phtml payload can be written under uploads/.
Identify that whether the written file executes depends on the web-server handler for uploads/, which is not in the reviewed source; do not assume the host blocks or allows PHP execution there.

Record the execution result of issue 2 as needs_validation with that exact blocker and a safe validation plan (owner confirms the uploads/ handler, or reproduce on a disposable local stack with the recorded server config), assigning no severity to the unconfirmed execution claim.

State what the source alone establishes for issue 2 (an upload_files user can write an attacker-chosen extension into a web-accessible uploads/ path) and the missing fact that decides its impact. Rate it as confirmed only if a concrete result is demonstrated independent of host configuration; otherwise keep it needs_validation. A clearly labeled conditional rating (for example, High if PHP executes) is acceptable guidance but must not enter confirmed totals.

Recommend concrete fixes for issue 2: validate extension and content with wp_check_filetype_and_ext() against an allowlist, sanitize the filename, and store through wp_handle_sideload() or media_handle_sideload().
Do not copy the scanner's High ratings; justify each severity from demonstrated impact and reachability, and keep needs_validation and rejected items out of confirmed severity totals.
success_criteria: Issue 1 is not reported as a confirmed High stored-XSS finding; the report explains that the unfiltered_html capability check limits the write to principals already trusted with raw HTML, and records it as rejected or hardening without severity unless a lower-trust path is shown.
Issue 2's code-execution claim is recorded as needs_validation with the exact server-configuration blocker and a safe validation plan, and carries no severity.

Issue 2's report names the lower-trust principal (upload_files), the failed control (header-only MIME check), and the affected path; any severity is either justified against the anchors for a demonstrated result or explicitly conditional on the named blocker, never copied from the scanner label.
The report includes concrete remediation using wp_check_filetype_and_ext() or equivalent extension-and-content validation and a WordPress sideload API.
Confirmed severity totals exclude needs_validation, rejected, and hardening items, and no live-site probing is proposed.
